bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Climate change, energy efficiency and emissions — Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk with negative financial implications. Increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events can cause disruption in airport operations, and airport-specific climate adaptation is treated as essential to bolster resilience to present and future climate risks; the sector's disruption from climate change is said to influence the entire global economy.
- Safety and security of passengers and employees — Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk with negative implications. Poor safety and security leads to occupational hazards, disruption in airport operations and penalties from the regulatory bodies; the Company mitigates through surveillance, emergency response plans, regular safety audits and alignment with DGCA and ICAO standards.
- Cybersecurity and data privacy — Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk with negative implications. Increasing reliance on digital technologies and the interconnectedness of operating systems can lead to cybersecurity breaches, data privacy violations and reputational damage, and data breaches can seriously impact reputation and disrupt financial stability - mitigated by a cybersecurity and data privacy programme, incident response plans, monthly IT security training and internal audits.
- Stakeholder engagement and community relations — Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as both a risk and an opportunity. Poor stakeholder engagement and community relations can lead to negative public perception, social unrest and legal challenges affecting the reputation and financial performance of the airport sector; strong relationships conversely support brand loyalty, workforce retention, revenue and profitability.
- Geopolitical conflict, fuel cost and airspace disruption — Management notes that the outbreak of armed conflict in West Asia carries direct consequences for the aviation sector through elevated fuel costs and airspace closures leading to longer and less economical route diversions, with Brent crude crossing USD 110 per barrel after hostilities began. The continued closure of Pakistani airspace to Indian commercial carriers has had a major operational impact, lengthening flight times and raising fuel burn on westbound international routes.
- Currency depreciation and foreign-currency exposure — The Indian Rupee depreciated by over 11% against the US Dollar during FY 2025-26, the steepest annual fall since FY 2011-12, breaching Rs 95 per USD, alongside a merchandise trade deficit widening to USD 333.2 Bn. The Group carries US Dollar-denominated borrowings - GHIAL's 15-year rupee NCD issue was explicitly aimed at eliminating currency risk on the refinanced borrowing - so unhedged foreign-currency debt and dollar-linked costs are a structural exposure.
- Business and geographic concentration in a small number of airport concessions — The BRSR shows 87.48% of turnover from development and operations of airport assets and 6.48% from allied city-side real estate and security services, with operations in only 5 states and 3 international countries and exports at 6.40% of standalone turnover. Group performance is therefore concentrated in a handful of concession assets - principally Delhi and Hyderabad - so an event at any one gateway, or a concession or regulatory change affecting it, is material to the whole platform.
- Rising employee attrition and talent retention — The BRSR turnover-rate disclosure shows permanent employee turnover rising to 17% in FY 2026 from 13% in FY 2025 and 12% in FY 2024, with female permanent-employee turnover at 25%. Sustained attrition at that pace is a structural execution risk for a business scaling several new airports, adjacency verticals and an MRO platform simultaneously.

business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: GMR Airports Limited develops, operates and manages airports under long-tenure concessions, principally Delhi (IGIA), Hyderabad (RGIA), Goa (Manohar International Airport at Mopa), Nagpur and Bidar in India, with overseas exposure through Medan (Indonesia), Crete (Greece) and technical services to Mactan Cebu in the Philippines. Beyond regulated aeronautical operations, it runs an expanding set of airport-adjacency businesses - duty free, cargo, retail, food and beverage, car parking, advertising, forex, hospitality and lounges - together with Airport Land Development on its city-side land banks at Delhi Aerocity and Aerocity Hyderabad, and India's largest third-party MRO through GMR Air Cargo and Aerospace Engineering Limited. Customers span B2C, B2B and B2G segments, covering passengers and the organisations involved in air passenger, cargo transport and related operations.

- Grow Airport Land Development as a key strategic pillar, evolving from a traditional land-leasing model towards a value-accretive strategy of Build-to-Suit and higher-value self-development, with landmark office, hospitality, healthcare and industrial projects across Delhi and Hyderabad Aerocity and a widening pipeline at Goa and Bhogapuram.
- Transform airports into vibrant consumer destinations - India's first Gordon Ramsay restaurant at Delhi and a dedicated luxury retail cluster at Hyderabad featuring brands such as Chanel and Hugo Boss.
- Use technology as a differentiator: digital platforms, automation, data analytics and AI through the Unified Total Airside Management platform, predictive airport operations, advanced weather intelligence and enhanced digital passenger services, supported by GMR Innovex.
- Reinforce cybersecurity resilience through a 24x7 integrated cyber defence framework protecting critical digital infrastructure and uninterrupted operations.
- Keep sustainability at the heart of the growth strategy through leadership in carbon management, renewable energy adoption, resource efficiency and resilient infrastructure.
- Strengthen governance and trust via a well-defined Family Governance model, the GMR Group's seven core values, structured internal audit with independent external review, and a Contract Lifecycle Management platform for contract governance and compliance.
- Expand presence in the Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul sector over time as the aviation ecosystem creates significant MRO opportunities.
- Explore airport and adjacency opportunities beyond India in emerging markets across West Asia, Central Asia, Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia.

outlook.body: FY 2025-26 was a year of portfolio expansion and capacity build-out across GAL's airport platform. In greenfield development, GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Limited took construction of Bhogapuram International Airport substantially ahead of the original schedule, reaching 99.73% physical progress by June 30, 2026 with the validation flight completed and the airport declared a 'Major Airport' by AERA; it was inaugurated on August 1, 2026 and is to commence commercial operations in August 2026 with 6 MPPA initial capacity expandable to a maximum of 40 MPPA, a 3,800-metre CAT I enabled runway and LEED Platinum pre-certification. The new international airport at Heraklion, Crete, built in partnership with Terna S.A., reached approximately 74% overall progress by June 2026; the project is fully funded, principally through the State Grant already received and the Airport Modernisation & Development Tax, and remains debt-free, representing the first instance of an Indian airport operator winning a concession to build and operate a European airport. Portfolio additions included the operational takeover of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar International Airport, Nagpur on June 25, 2026 by GNIAL under the October 2024 concession with MIHAN India Limited, with phased development planned to enhance passenger and cargo handling capacity. At Delhi, organic capacity was expanded through recommissioning of CAT III-capable Runway 10/28, inauguration of the upgraded Terminal 2 (reopened in October 2025) and conversion of Pier C at Terminal 3 into an international pier, which raised Terminal 3's annual international capacity and took the airport's realigned annual terminal capacity to 105 million passengers, while airside capacity rose from 1,522 to 1,700 ATMs per day and wide-body stand availability for international operations improved by approximately 40%. At Hyderabad, GHIAL commissioned Cargo Terminal 2 with initial handling capacity of approximately 50,000 MT per annum and dedicated expansion areas to scale to 100,000 MTPA, including a fully temperature-controlled pharma zone, and the Safran engine MRO facility was handed over within the Aerocity ecosystem. The adjacency platform moved from concession wins to operating reality, with duty free operations commencing at Delhi from July 28, 2025 and Hyderabad from September 10, 2025, the Cargo Terminal 1 concession at Delhi formally awarded in March 2026, and Selected Bidder status in August 2025 for the Cargo City at Delhi covering 50.5 acres of cargo and logistics facilities. GACAEL's MRO base at Hyderabad is near full utilisation with a hangar expansion programme planned. On funding, capital allocation priorities remain focused on funding committed growth projects, scaling adjacency businesses and maintaining flexibility for future airport opportunities, supported during the year by balance-sheet strengthening, maturity extension and cost-of-capital reduction across GHIAL, DIAL and the corporate entity.

outlook.body:
- A long runway of growth for the portfolio supported by long residual concession tenures and strong underlying demand fundamentals.
- Growing non-aeronautical revenue streams and the successful integration of the Cargo and Duty-Free businesses strengthening the Company's revenue streams.
- Commencement of operations at Nagpur International Airport after the close of FY 2025-26, described as a new engine of value creation.
- India's widening lattice of trade agreements - nine FTAs spanning 38 countries, with EFTA TEPA, India-UK CETA, India-Oman CEPA and India-New Zealand - expected to translate directly into long-haul passenger flows, air cargo volumes and route development at India's gateway airports.
- The Government's vision of positioning India as a global aviation hub through a hub-and-spoke model, with Delhi already India's first hub-and-spoke gateway via Varanasi and Amritsar and further regional airports to be integrated over time.
- Long-term growth of Indian aviation supported by rising incomes, expanding tourism, increasing penetration of aviation infrastructure and progressive government initiatives.
- Large fleet expansion plans by Indian carriers and the emergence of the aircraft leasing ecosystem at GIFT City, expected to enhance industry competitiveness and support sustained traffic growth.
- The expanding aviation ecosystem creating significant opportunities in the MRO sector.
- Global aviation industry expansion across emerging markets in West Asia, Central Asia, Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia, offering opportunities for airports and adjacent businesses.
- Headwind: the West Asia conflict carrying direct consequences for aviation through elevated fuel costs and airspace closures leading to longer and less economical route diversions.
- Headwind: continued closure of Pakistani airspace to Indian commercial carriers, lengthening flight times and raising fuel burn on westbound international routes.
- Headwind: Indian Rupee depreciation of over 11% against the US Dollar in FY 2025-26 and Brent crude crossing USD 110 per barrel after the outbreak of hostilities.
- Macro backdrop: India's real GDP grew 7.7% in FY 2025-26 with public capital expenditure sustained near Rs 11 Lakh Crore, while the IMF projects global growth slowing to 3.0% in 2026 with risks decisively on the downside.
- India entering FY 2026-27 with strong domestic fundamentals but a more challenging external environment, with medium-term drivers - demographics, rising discretionary incomes, public infrastructure investment and new trade agreements - firmly intact.
- Greenfield pipeline: Bhogapuram International Airport at 99.73% physical progress as of June 30, 2026 with all key regulatory approvals secured, poised to commence commercial operations during August 2026.
- Cargo City at Delhi International Airport - GAL emerged as Selected Bidder in August 2025 for development of cargo and logistics facilities over 50.5 acres.
- Cargo Terminal 1 at Delhi International Airport - concession formally awarded to GAL in March 2026 to upgrade, modernise, finance, operate, manage and maintain the terminal.
- Nagpur International Airport concession with MIHAN India Limited (signed October 2024), with phased development planned to enhance passenger and cargo handling capacity.
- Airport Land Development pipeline of landmark office, hospitality, healthcare and industrial projects across Delhi and Hyderabad Aerocity, with the development pipeline further expanded at Goa and Bhogapuram.

risks.note: The Indian Rupee depreciated by over 11% against the US Dollar during FY 2025-26, the steepest annual fall since FY 2011-12, breaching Rs 95 per USD, alongside a merchandise trade deficit widening to USD 333.2 Bn. The Group carries US Dollar-denominated borrowings - GHIAL's 15-year rupee NCD issue was explicitly aimed at eliminating currency risk on the refinanced borrowing - so unhedged foreign-currency debt and dollar-linked costs are a structural exposure.

The BRSR shows 87.48% of turnover from development and operations of airport assets and 6.48% from allied city-side real estate and security services, with operations in only 5 states and 3 international countries and exports at 6.40% of standalone turnover. Group performance is therefore concentrated in a handful of concession assets - principally Delhi and Hyderabad - so an event at any one gateway, or a concession or regulatory change affecting it, is material to the whole platform.
risks.risk: Business and geographic concentration in a small number of airport concessions

risks.note: The BRSR turnover-rate disclosure shows permanent employee turnover rising to 17% in FY 2026 from 13% in FY 2025 and 12% in FY 2024, with female permanent-employee turnover at 25%. currentContext.expansion: FY 2025-26 was a year of portfolio expansion and capacity build-out across GAL's airport platform. In greenfield development, GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Limited took construction of Bhogapuram International Airport substantially ahead of the original schedule, reaching 99.73% physical progress by June 30, 2026 with the validation flight completed and the airport declared a 'Major Airport' by AERA; it was inaugurated on August 1, 2026 and is to commence commercial operations in August 2026 with 6 MPPA initial capacity expandable to a maximum of 40 MPPA, a 3,800-metre CAT I enabled runway and LEED Platinum pre-certification. The new international airport at Heraklion, Crete, built in partnership with Terna S.A., reached approximately 74% overall progress by June 2026; the project is fully funded, principally through the State Grant already received and the Airport Modernisation & Development Tax, and remains debt-free, representing the first instance of an Indian airport operator winning a concession to build and operate a European airport. Portfolio additions included the operational takeover of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar International Airport, Nagpur on June 25, 2026 by GNIAL under the October 2024 concession with MIHAN India Limited, with phased development planned to enhance passenger and cargo handling capacity. At Delhi, organic capacity was expanded through recommissioning of CAT III-capable Runway 10/28, inauguration of the upgraded Terminal 2 (reopened in October 2025) and conversion of Pier C at Terminal 3 into an international pier, which raised Terminal 3's annual international capacity and took the airport's realigned annual terminal capacity to 105 million passengers, while airside capacity rose from 1,522 to 1,700 ATMs per day and wide-body stand availability for international operations improved by approximately 40%. At Hyderabad, GHIAL commissioned Cargo Terminal 2 with initial handling capacity of approximately 50,000 MT per annum and dedicated expansion areas to scale to 100,000 MTPA, including a fully temperature-controlled pharma zone, and the Safran engine MRO facility was handed over within the Aerocity ecosystem. The adjacency platform moved from concession wins to operating reality, with duty free operations commencing at Delhi from July 28, 2025 and Hyderabad from September 10, 2025, the Cargo Terminal 1 concession at Delhi formally awarded in March 2026, and Selected Bidder status in August 2025 for the Cargo City at Delhi covering 50.5 acres of cargo and logistics facilities. GACAEL's MRO base at Hyderabad is near full utilisation with a hangar expansion programme planned. On funding, capital allocation priorities remain focused on funding committed growth projects, scaling adjacency businesses and maintaining flexibility for future airport opportunities, supported during the year by balance-sheet strengthening, maturity extension and cost-of-capital reduction across GHIAL, DIAL and the corporate entity.

risks.risk: Climate change, energy efficiency and emissions
risks.note: Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk with negative financial implications. Increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events can cause disruption in airport operations, and airport-specific climate adaptation is treated as essential to bolster resilience to present and future climate risks; the sector's disruption from climate change is said to influence the entire global economy.

risks.risk: Safety and security of passengers and employees
risks.note: Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk with negative implications. Poor safety and security leads to occupational hazards, disruption in airport operations and penalties from the regulatory bodies; the Company mitigates through surveillance, emergency response plans, regular safety audits and alignment with DGCA and ICAO standards.

Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as a risk with negative implications. Increasing reliance on digital technologies and the interconnectedness of operating systems can lead to cybersecurity breaches, data privacy violations and reputational damage, and data breaches can seriously impact reputation and disrupt financial stability - mitigated by a cybersecurity and data privacy programme, incident response plans, monthly IT security training and internal audits.

Identified in the BRSR material-issues table as both a risk and an opportunity. Poor stakeholder engagement and community relations can lead to negative public perception, social unrest and legal challenges affecting the reputation and financial performance of the airport sector; strong relationships conversely support brand loyalty, workforce retention, revenue and profitability.

risks.risk: Geopolitical conflict, fuel cost and airspace disruption
risks.note: Management notes that the outbreak of armed conflict in West Asia carries direct consequences for the aviation sector through elevated fuel costs and airspace closures leading to longer and less economical route diversions, with Brent crude crossing USD 110 per barrel after hostilities began. The continued closure of Pakistani airspace to Indian commercial carriers has had a major operational impact, lengthening flight times and raising fuel burn on westbound international routes.

The Indian Rupee depreciated by over 11% against the US Dollar during FY 2025-26, the steepest annual fall since FY 2011-12, breaching Rs 95 per USD, alongside a merchandise trade deficit widening to USD 333.2 Bn. The Group carries US Dollar-denominated borrowings - GHIAL's 15-year rupee NCD issue was explicitly aimed at eliminating currency risk on the refinanced borrowing - so unhedged foreign-currency debt and dollar-linked costs are a structural exposure.

risks.risk: Business and geographic concentration in a small number of airport concessions
risks.note: The BRSR shows 87.48% of turnover from development and operations of airport assets and 6.48% from allied city-side real estate and security services, with operations in only 5 states and 3 international countries and exports at 6.40% of standalone turnover. Group performance is therefore concentrated in a handful of concession assets - principally Delhi and Hyderabad - so an event at any one gateway, or a concession or regulatory change affecting it, is material to the whole platform.

risks.risk: Rising employee attrition and talent retention
risks.note: The BRSR turnover-rate disclosure shows permanent employee turnover rising to 17% in FY 2026 from 13% in FY 2025 and 12% in FY 2024, with female permanent-employee turnover at 25%. Sustained attrition at that pace is a structural execution risk for a business scaling several new airports, adjacency verticals and an MRO platform simultaneously.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: GMR Airports Limited develops, operates and manages airports under long-tenure concessions, principally Delhi (IGIA), Hyderabad (RGIA), Goa (Manohar International Airport at Mopa), Nagpur and Bidar in India, with overseas exposure through Medan (Indonesia), Crete (Greece) and technical services to Mactan Cebu in the Philippines. Beyond regulated aeronautical operations, it runs an expanding set of airport-adjacency businesses - duty free, cargo, retail, food and beverage, car parking, advertising, forex, hospitality and lounges - together with Airport Land Development on its city-side land banks at Delhi Aerocity and Aerocity Hyderabad, and India's largest third-party MRO through GMR Air Cargo and Aerospace Engineering Limited. Customers span B2C, B2B and B2G segments, covering passengers and the organisations involved in air passenger, cargo transport and related operations.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- A long runway of growth for the portfolio supported by long residual concession tenures and strong underlying demand fundamentals.
- Growing non-aeronautical revenue streams and the successful integration of the Cargo and Duty-Free businesses strengthening the Company's revenue streams.
- Commencement of operations at Nagpur International Airport after the close of FY 2025-26, described as a new engine of value creation.
- India's widening lattice of trade agreements - nine FTAs spanning 38 countries, with EFTA TEPA, India-UK CETA, India-Oman CEPA and India-New Zealand - expected to translate directly into long-haul passenger flows, air cargo volumes and route development at India's gateway airports.
- The Government's vision of positioning India as a global aviation hub through a hub-and-spoke model, with Delhi already India's first hub-and-spoke gateway via Varanasi and Amritsar and further regional airports to be integrated over time.
- Long-term growth of Indian aviation supported by rising incomes, expanding tourism, increasing penetration of aviation infrastructure and progressive government initiatives.
- Large fleet expansion plans by Indian carriers and the emergence of the aircraft leasing ecosystem at GIFT City, expected to enhance industry competitiveness and support sustained traffic growth.
- The expanding aviation ecosystem creating significant opportunities in the MRO sector.
- Global aviation industry expansion across emerging markets in West Asia, Central Asia, Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia, offering opportunities for airports and adjacent businesses.
- Headwind: the West Asia conflict carrying direct consequences for aviation through elevated fuel costs and airspace closures leading to longer and less economical route diversions.
- Headwind: continued closure of Pakistani airspace to Indian commercial carriers, lengthening flight times and raising fuel burn on westbound international routes.
- Headwind: Indian Rupee depreciation of over 11% against the US Dollar in FY 2025-26 and Brent crude crossing USD 110 per barrel after the outbreak of hostilities.
- Macro backdrop: India's real GDP grew 7.7% in FY 2025-26 with public capital expenditure sustained near Rs 11 Lakh Crore, while the IMF projects global growth slowing to 3.0% in 2026 with risks decisively on the downside.
- India entering FY 2026-27 with strong domestic fundamentals but a more challenging external environment, with medium-term drivers - demographics, rising discretionary incomes, public infrastructure investment and new trade agreements - firmly intact.
- Greenfield pipeline: Bhogapuram International Airport at 99.73% physical progress as of June 30, 2026 with all key regulatory approvals secured, poised to commence commercial operations during August 2026.
- Cargo City at Delhi International Airport - GAL emerged as Selected Bidder in August 2025 for development of cargo and logistics facilities over 50.5 acres.
- Cargo Terminal 1 at Delhi International Airport - concession formally awarded to GAL in March 2026 to upgrade, modernise, finance, operate, manage and maintain the terminal.
- Nagpur International Airport concession with MIHAN India Limited (signed October 2024), with phased development planned to enhance passenger and cargo handling capacity.
- Airport Land Development pipeline of landmark office, hospitality, healthcare and industrial projects across Delhi and Hyderabad Aerocity, with the development pipeline further expanded at Goa and Bhogapuram.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY 2025-26 was a year of portfolio expansion and capacity build-out across GAL's airport platform. In greenfield development, GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Limited took construction of Bhogapuram International Airport substantially ahead of the original schedule, reaching 99.73% physical progress by June 30, 2026 with the validation flight completed and the airport declared a 'Major Airport' by AERA; it was inaugurated on August 1, 2026 and is to commence commercial operations in August 2026 with 6 MPPA initial capacity expandable to a maximum of 40 MPPA, a 3,800-metre CAT I enabled runway and LEED Platinum pre-certification. The new international airport at Heraklion, Crete, built in partnership with Terna S.A., reached approximately 74% overall progress by June 2026; the project is fully funded, principally through the State Grant already received and the Airport Modernisation & Development Tax, and remains debt-free, representing the first instance of an Indian airport operator winning a concession to build and operate a European airport. Portfolio additions included the operational takeover of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar International Airport, Nagpur on June 25, 2026 by GNIAL under the October 2024 concession with MIHAN India Limited, with phased development planned to enhance passenger and cargo handling capacity. At Delhi, organic capacity was expanded through recommissioning of CAT III-capable Runway 10/28, inauguration of the upgraded Terminal 2 (reopened in October 2025) and conversion of Pier C at Terminal 3 into an international pier, which raised Terminal 3's annual international capacity and took the airport's realigned annual terminal capacity to 105 million passengers, while airside capacity rose from 1,522 to 1,700 ATMs per day and wide-body stand availability for international operations improved by approximately 40%. At Hyderabad, GHIAL commissioned Cargo Terminal 2 with initial handling capacity of approximately 50,000 MT per annum and dedicated expansion areas to scale to 100,000 MTPA, including a fully temperature-controlled pharma zone, and the Safran engine MRO facility was handed over within the Aerocity ecosystem. The adjacency platform moved from concession wins to operating reality, with duty free operations commencing at Delhi from July 28, 2025 and Hyderabad from September 10, 2025, the Cargo Terminal 1 concession at Delhi formally awarded in March 2026, and Selected Bidder status in August 2025 for the Cargo City at Delhi covering 50.5 acres of cargo and logistics facilities. GACAEL's MRO base at Hyderabad is near full utilisation with a hangar expansion programme planned. On funding, capital allocation priorities remain focused on funding committed growth projects, scaling adjacency businesses and maintaining flexibility for future airport opportunities, supported during the year by balance-sheet strengthening, maturity extension and cost-of-capital reduction across GHIAL, DIAL and the corporate entity.

themes.title: Hospitality & travel up-cycle
themes.need: Q1FY27 split hotels from airlines. INDHOTEL delivered a 17th consecutive record quarter - consolidated revenue INR 2,419cr (+15%), EBITDA INR 753cr at 31.1%, standalone occupancy jumping to 82% from 76% on a 41.8% standalone EBITDA margin, and asset-light management-fee income INR 168cr (+26%) - with management now framing the West-Asia war as a NET tailwind because outbound travel stays home; leisure RevPAR (Rajasthan/Goa) ran up high-20s. Airlines got the mirror image: INDIGO's EBITDAR margin collapsed from 28.0% to 15.6% on blended ATF of ~INR 140-150/litre versus INR 85-90 pre-war (fuel CASK +~80% YoY), leaving yield as the only defence. MHRIL shows domestic leisure premiumisation is real - Keystone average unit realisation +73% to INR 14.4 lakh on stable gross sales. LEMONTREE/CHALET/SAMHI/THELEELA ride the same occupancy-led room cycle; TRAVELFOOD/TBOTEK/DREAMFOLKS remain levered to airport PAX and B2B travel.
themes.driver: Occupancy-led (not rate-led) RevPAR compounding plus INDHOTEL's Ginger conversion cadence stepping 15->20->25->40 per quarter through FY27; for airlines the swing is INDIGO's guided Q2 PRASK growth of 'more than 25%' on flattish capacity against ATF cracks.
